cognate: Gk εὐρύς = Ved. urú- (*h₁urú-, 'wide'); Gk πόντος = Ved. pánthā-/path- (*pónteh₂s/*pnth₂-, 'way, passage'): both members cognate
drift_or_renewal: drift in Greek: πόντος has narrowed from 'passage, way across' to 'open sea' (the sea as the way to be crossed); Vedic keeps 'path, road'. The adjective is unchanged.
shared_syntax: attributive adjective + noun in agreement (Ved. urúḥ pánthāḥ, urúm ... pánthām, pathā́ urúṇā, uraú pathí; Hom. εὐρέα πόντον, εὐρέι πόντῳ), typically as goal or medium of a verb of travelling (Ved. √sṛj 'run' 4.26.5, ráthāya 'for the chariot' 8.68.13; Gk ἐπιπλέω, περάω, ἐνίημι 'launch into'). CAVEAT: in the slab's Greek anchor (Hesiod Op. 246-7 as quoted by Aeschines) εὐρὺν agrees with στρατὸν and πόντῳ is bare; the two words share the hexameter sentence but not the phrase. The agreeing Greek collocation is in the support (Homer x9, Hesiod x2, HH Ap., Soph.). RV 5.1.11c (urú there agrees with antárikṣam) is left out of the anchors.
context: In both traditions the phrase names an expanse traversed by a vehicle: the Vedic wide path is driven by chariot or steed (of the gods, of Dakṣiṇā, the mind-swift horse); the Homeric wide pontos is sailed across (ἐπιπλὼς, ἐπέπλων, περήσαμεν) or is where ships are launched (ἐνήσομεν). The Greek uses with verbs of crossing keep the old 'way' sense of πόντος alive, so the contexts line up.
phrase: *h₁urúm pónteh₂m 'the wide way': Ved. urúḥ pánthāḥ ~ Gk εὐρὺς πόντος
note: Why this is probably not chance: of the adjectives that go with πόντος in Homer, εὐρύς is the third most common (9 lines, after ἰχθυόεις 13 and ἠεροειδής 11), and those lines are concentrated in voyage contexts. Why it might be generic: both 'wide' adjectives are stock epithets of large spaces (εὐρεῖα χθών, urú antárikṣam), so they could have been put with the noun independently. The pontos/pánthāḥ etymology and the 'passage' meaning of πόντος (Benveniste) come from the literature.

support.locus: AVŚ 1.35.4; 2.13.3; 6.78.6 (and c. 50 AV sentences with dīrgha + āyus, many dīrghāyutvāya)
compound: Gk μακραίων (5x in GLAUx poetry) ~ Ved. dīrghā́yu-/dīrghā́yuṣ- (RV)

cognate: noun: Ved. ā́yus-/āyu-, Av. āiiu-, Gk αἰών (all *h₂óyu-/*h₂eyu- 'life-force, lifetime'); adjective: Ved. dīrghá- = Av. darəga- (*dl̥h₁gʰó- 'long')
drift_or_renewal: renewal in Greek: the inherited 'long' adjective (*dl̥h₁gʰó-, Gk δολιχός) does not occur with αἰών in the searched Greek (0 hits); μακρός/μήκιστος (*meh₂ḱ-) or δηρόν (Il. 9.415) stands in its place. Indo-Iranian keeps the cognate pair (Ved. dīrghám ā́yuḥ = GAv. darəgə̄m āiiū, Y 31.20).
shared_syntax: 'long' adjective agreeing with or governing the 'lifetime' noun as an object or measure of a person's life: Ved. dīrghám ā́yuḥ kṛṇotu 'may he make a long life' (object, accusative); Gk ἐπὶ τὸ μήκιστον ἀνθρωπίνου αἰῶνος 'to the longest span of human life' (partitive genitive after a superlative); poetic Gk μακρὸς αἰών / δι' αἰῶνος μακροῦ (attributive). The Greek anchors are Xenophon prose: the adjective is a superlative there, not an attribute.
context: Both are about a person's allotted lifespan running its full length: the AV verse is a prayer for long life (with prajā and dhana); Xenophon is describing Agesilaus reaching the longest span of human life and dying in old age; Il. 9.415 sets 'long life' (δηρὸν ... αἰών) against undying fame. The noun keeps its old meaning 'vital span' in both.
phrase: *dl̥h₁gʰóm h₂óyu 'long life': Ved. dīrghám ā́yuḥ = Av. darəgə̄m āiiū ~ Gk (renewed) μακρὸς αἰών / μήκιστος αἰών
note: The Indo-Iranian pair is a strong exact match (10 RV padas, about 50 AV sentences, Y 31.20). The Greek side is weaker: one cognate only, and 'long life' is semantically transparent, so it could have been coined independently. In its favour, the noun used is specifically the inherited lifespan word in its old sense, and the compounds Gk μακραίων ~ Ved. dīrghā́yu- run in parallel. No Latin longum aeuum was found in LASLA.

All 226 bundles read (all pivots Greek prose/poetry from GLAUx; partners mostly Cato, Lucretius, Plautus, AV, RV). Most bundles hold only generic shared roots (numerals, pater/mater, do/facio, possum). Two medium claims: urú- pánthā- ~ εὐρὺς πόντος (drift of πόντος), and dīrghám ā́yuḥ ~ μακρὸς/μήκιστος αἰών (adjective renewed in Greek). Considered and rejected: σπονδαί/σπένδομαι ~ spondeo (shared institutional vocabulary, no shared phrase); ἄγειν καὶ φέρειν (no Latin ago+fero formula in LASLA); ἄροτρον καὶ ζυγόν ~ aratra/iuga (Cato's inventory lists, generic); Ἡλίου ἅρμα ~ solis meatus (second member not cognate).
